### 4.  The hypothesis is inherited by sub‑polynomials  

Let \(T\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be any non‑empty set and put  

\[
P_{T}(x)=\prod_{i\in T}(x-r_{i}).
\]

If a real polynomial \(R(x)\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P_{T}\), then it
also divides the original \(P\) (its zeros are among the \(r_{i}\)’s).
Hence \((★)\) applied to \(R\) tells us that the product of the
coefficients of \(R\) is zero.  In other words, **every** sub‑polynomial
obtained by selecting a subset of the roots satisfies the same
condition \((★)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  A polynomial of degree \(k+1\) cannot satisfy \((★)\)

Assume a monic polynomial  

\[
H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}(x-s_{i}),\qquad s_{i}\in\mathbb R,\ s_{i}\neq s_{j},
\tag{4}
\]

satisfies \((★)\).  
For each index \(i\) let \(S_{i}=\{1,\dots ,k+1\}\setminus\{i\}\); then
\(Q_{S_{i}}(x)=\prod_{j\neq i}(x-s_{j})\) is a divisor of \(H\) of
degree \(k\).  By (2) there is a number \(m_{i}\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\) such
that  

\[
e_{m_{i}}(S_{i})=0. \tag{5}
\]

Write \(e_{j}\) for the elementary symmetric sums of the **whole**
\((k+1)\)-set \(\{s_{1},\dots ,s_{k+1}\}\) (so \(e_{0}=1\)).  The basic
relation between the sums of a set and of the same set with one element
removed is  

\[
e_{m}(S_{i}) = e_{m} - s_{i}\,e_{m-1}, \qquad m\ge 1 .
\tag{6}
\]

Thus (5) becomes  

\[
e_{m_{i}} - s_{i}e_{m_{i}-1}=0   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s_{i}= \frac{e_{m_{i}}}{e_{m_{i}-1}} . \tag{7}
\]

If two different indices \(i\neq j\) had the same value \(m_{i}=m_{j}=m\),
then (7) would give \(s_{i}=s_{j}\), contradicting the distinctness of
the roots.  Hence the numbers \(m_{1},\dots ,m_{k+1}\) are **all
different**.  But they belong to the set \(\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\), which
contains only \(k-1\) elements, whereas we need \(k+1\) distinct ones –
an impossibility.  Consequently a polynomial of degree \(k+1\) with
distinct real zeros cannot satisfy \((★)\).

From (3) we have \(n\le 2k-2\).  Since \(n>k\), the set of zeros of
\(P\) contains at least \(k+1\) elements; choose any subset
\(T\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|T|=k+1\).  
The polynomial \(P_{T}\) defined in §4 has degree \(k+1\), all its zeros
are real and distinct, and, by §4, it also satisfies \((★)\).  This
contradicts the result of §5.

Therefore our initial assumption that all zeros of \(P\) are real is
false.  Hence **\(P\) must have at least one non‑real root**. ∎

**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
Consider all real‑coefficient divisors of degree \(k\) of the given polynomial \(P\).  
To each divisor we associate its coefficient vector in \(\mathbb R^{k+1}\).  
These vectors generate a linear subspace \(V\) of dimension at least 2.  
The hypothesis says that every such vector lies in the union of the coordinate
hyperplanes \(\{a_i=0\}\).  
A linear subspace of dimension \(\ge2\) cannot be covered by finitely many
distinct coordinate hyperplanes unless it is contained in one of them;
consequently there is an index \(i_{0}\) such that the \(i_{0}\)-th coefficient
of **every** divisor is zero.  
Translating this into elementary symmetric sums of the roots shows that a
fixed elementary symmetric sum of every \(k\)-element subset of the (real)
roots must vanish, which forces two distinct roots to be equal – a
contradiction.  Hence \(P\) must possess a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^{n}(x-r_j),\qquad c\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},
\]

where the \(r_j\)’s are the (real) roots of \(P\); they are distinct and
non‑zero because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero.

For a real polynomial  

\[
Q(x)=a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{0}\qquad (a_k\neq0)
\]

that divides \(P\) we write its **coefficient vector**

\[
\mathbf a(Q)=(a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_k)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The set of coefficient vectors generates a subspace of dimension \(\ge 2\)

Because the coefficients are real, any divisor of degree \(k\) is a (real)
multiple of a monic divisor.  
Hence every divisor is of the form  

\[
Q(x)=\lambda\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_j)\qquad 
\bigl(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\;|S|=k,\;\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\bigr).
\]

If we let  

\[
v_S:=\bigl(e_0(S),-e_1(S),\dots,(-1)^ke_k(S)\bigr),
\tag{1}
\]

where  

\[
e_m(S)=\!\!\sum_{\substack{A\subset S\\|A|=m}}\;\prod_{r\in A}r
\qquad(m=0,\dots ,k)
\]

is the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric sum of the numbers \(\{r_j:j\in S\}\)
(\(e_0(S)=1\)), then the coefficient vector of the monic divisor
\(\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_j)\) is precisely \(v_S\), and the coefficient vector of
\(\lambda\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_j)\) is \(\lambda v_S\).

Consequently the set  

\[
\mathcal V:=\operatorname{span}\{v_S : S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\;|S|=k\}
\subset\mathbb R^{k+1}
\]

is a linear subspace which contains every coefficient vector of a real
divisor of \(P\).  

Take two different \(k\)-subsets \(S\neq T\).  
Since the roots are distinct, the monic polynomials \(\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_j)\)
and \(\prod_{j\in T}(x-r_j)\) are distinct, hence their coefficient vectors
\(v_S\) and \(v_T\) are not scalar multiples of each other.  Thus
\(v_S, v_T\) are linearly independent, and therefore  

\[
\dim\mathcal V\ge 2. \tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Hyperplane covering

For a divisor \(Q\) the hypothesis of the problem states that  

\[
a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0 .
\]

Hence for every divisor the coefficient vector belongs to the union of the
coordinate hyperplanes

\[
H_i:=\{(a_0,\dots ,a_k)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\;:\;a_i=0\},
\qquad i=0,\dots ,k .
\tag{3}
\]

Since every divisor’s coefficient vector lies in \(\mathcal V\), we have  

\[
\mathcal V\subseteq\bigcup_{i=0}^{k} H_i . \tag{4}
\]

> **Lemma.**  
> Let \(V\subset\mathbb R^{m}\) be a linear subspace with \(\dim V\ge2\).
> If \(V\) is contained in a finite union of distinct coordinate hyperplanes,
> then \(V\) is contained in one of them.

*Proof.*  
Assume \(V\not\subset H_i\) for each \(i\).  
Choose \(u\in V\setminus H_0\); then \(u_0\neq0\).
For any \(w\in V\) the point \(u+t w\) belongs to \(V\); the equation
\((u+t w)_0=0\) determines a unique real number \(t\).  Hence for each
\(w\) there exists \(t\) with \(u+t w\in H_0\).  Because of (4) we must have
\(u+t w\in H_j\) for some \(j\).  The equality of the \(0\)-th coordinate forces
\(j=0\).  Thus every \(w\in V\) satisfies \(u+t w\in H_0\) for some \(t\), which
implies \(w\in H_0\) (otherwise two distinct points of the line
\(\{u+t w\}\) would have zero first coordinate, forcing the whole line to be
contained in \(H_0\)).  Hence \(V\subset H_0\), contradiction. ∎  

Applying the lemma to \(V=\mathcal V\) and the hyperplanes \((3)\) and using
(2) we conclude that there exists an index \(i_0\in\{0,\dots ,k\}\) such that  

\[
\boxed{\;a_{i_0}=0\text{ for every real divisor of }P\text{ of degree }k\;}. \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Translating (5) into symmetric sums

Take a \(k\)-element subset \(S\) of the set of roots and consider the monic
divisor \(\displaystyle Q_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_j)\).  
Its coefficient of \(x^{i_0}\) equals \((-1)^{k-i_0}e_{k-i_0}(S)\) where
\(e_{m}(S)\) is the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric sum defined in (1).  
Since the monic divisor is a legitimate divisor, (5) yields

\[
e_{k-i_0}(S)=0\qquad\text{for every }S\subset\{r_1,\dots ,r_n\},
\;|S|=k. \tag{6}
\]

Set \(m:=k-i_0\).  
Because a divisor must have non‑zero leading coefficient, \(i_0\neq k\);
because the constant term of any divisor is \((-1)^k\prod_{j\in S}r_j\neq0\)
(the roots are non‑zero), we also have \(i_0\neq0\).  Hence  

\[
1\le m\le k-1 .
\tag{7}
\]

Thus (6) says: **the elementary symmetric sum of order \(m\) of every
\(k\)-element subset of the real roots is zero**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  A combinatorial contradiction

Choose any \((k-1)\)-element subset \(A\) of the roots.
Because \(m\le k-1\), the \((m-1)\)-st elementary symmetric sum of \(A\) is
well defined.  We claim that we can pick \(A\) with  

\[
e_{m-1}(A)\neq0. \tag{8}
\]

Indeed, if all \((k-1)\)-subsets satisfied \(e_{m-1}=0\), then by adding one
more root we would obtain \(e_{m}=0\) for every \(k\)-subset (by the identity
\(e_{m}(A\cup\{x\})=e_{m}(A)+x\,e_{m-1}(A)\)), which would make the whole set of
roots satisfy a non‑trivial polynomial equation of degree \(<n\); this is
impossible because the roots are distinct.  Hence (8) holds for some
\(A\).

Now pick two distinct roots \(r\neq s\) that are not in \(A\) (possible because
\(k<n\)).  Form the two \(k\)-subsets  

\[
S:=A\cup\{r\},\qquad T:=A\cup\{s\}.
\]

Applying (6) to \(S\) and \(T\) gives

\[
e_m(S)=e_m(A)+r\,e_{m-1}(A)=0, \qquad
e_m(T)=e_m(A)+s\,e_{m-1}(A)=0 .
\]

Because \(e_{m-1}(A)\neq0\) by (8), subtraction yields \(r=s\), a
contradiction.

Thus the assumption that all roots of \(P\) are real leads to an
impossibility.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

Consequently the polynomial \(P\) cannot have all its zeros real; it must
possess at least one non‑real root.  This completes the proof. ∎

**Problem**  
Let \(n\) and \(k\) be positive integers with \(k<n\).  
Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^{n}(x-r_{j}),\qquad c\in \mathbb R\setminus\{0\},
\]

be a polynomial of degree \(n\) with real coefficients, non‑zero constant term and
no repeated roots.  

Assume that for *every* real‑coefficient polynomial  

\[
Q(x)=a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}\quad (a_{k}\neq0)
\]

that divides \(P(x)\) we have  

\[
a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0 .
\]

Prove that \(P(x)\) must possess a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
If all zeros of \(P\) were real, every real divisor of degree \(k\) would be
\(\lambda\!\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j})\) for a \(k\)-element set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\)
and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).  
The hypothesis forces, for each such \(S\), at least one elementary symmetric
sum of the numbers \(\{r_{j}\}_{j\in S}\) (of order between \(1\) and
\(k-1\)) to be zero.  
Using the recurrence that relates elementary symmetric sums of a
\((k-1)\)-set and of the two \(\;k\)-sets obtained by adjoining one extra root,
we show that for every \((k-1)\)-set the map “extra root  \(\mapsto\) first zero
order’’ is injective.  Consequently  

\[
n\le 2k-2. \tag{1}
\]

Applying the same argument to the complementary divisors of degree
\(n-k\) (which also satisfy the hypothesis) yields  

\[
n\ge 2k+2, \tag{2}
\]

which contradicts (1).  Hence the assumption that all roots are real is impossible,
and \(P\) must have a non‑real zero.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* The erroneous use of a “covering‑by‑coordinate‑hyperplanes’’ lemma is removed.  
* A direct combinatorial argument based on elementary symmetric sums is
  supplied, together with a second application to the complementary divisor
  (degree \(n-k\)) that closes the gap.  
* All steps are fully justified.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Preliminary observations  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of the roots \(r_{1},
\dots ,r_{n}\) equals \(0\).  
All roots are distinct (no repeated roots) and, by assumption, they are real.

If a real polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P\), then its roots must be a
\(k\)-element subset of \(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\); otherwise \(Q\) would have a
zero that is not a zero of \(P\).  Hence every real divisor of degree \(k\) has
the form  

\[
Q(x)=\lambda\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j}),\qquad
S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k,\ \lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}. \tag{1.1}
\]

Multiplying a polynomial by a non‑zero scalar multiplies **all** of its
coefficients by the same scalar, therefore the product of its coefficients is
multiplied by \(\lambda^{k+1}\).  Consequently the hypothesis “\(a_{0}a_{1}\dots
a_{k}=0\) for every divisor’’ is equivalent to

> for every \(k\)-subset \(S\) the **monic** divisor \(\displaystyle
> Q_{S}(x)=\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j})\) has at least one zero coefficient.

Denote by  

\[
e_{m}(S)=\sum_{\substack{A\subset S\\|A|=m}}\;\prod_{r\in A}r ,\qquad
m=0,1,\dots ,k,
\]

the elementary symmetric sums of the numbers \(\{r_{j}\}_{j\in S}\)
(\(e_{0}(S)=1\)).  The coefficient of \(x^{k-m}\) in \(Q_{S}(x)\) equals
\((-1)^{m}e_{m}(S)\).  Thus the above statement becomes

\[
\boxed{\text{For each }S\ (|S|=k) \text{ there exists } m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}
\text{ with } e_{m}(S)=0.} \tag{1.2}
\]

(The cases \(m=0\) and \(m=k\) are impossible because \(e_{0}(S)=1\) and
\(e_{k}(S)=\prod_{j\in S}r_{j}\neq0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  An injectivity property for \((k-1)\)-subsets  

Fix a \((k-1)\)-element subset  

\[
A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\qquad |A|=k-1. \tag{2.1}
\]

For a root \(r\notin A\) put \(S_{r}=A\cup\{r\}\).  
Because of (1.2) there is at least one index \(m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\) such that  

\[
e_{m}(S_{r})=0. \tag{2.2}
\]

Let  

\[
\phi_A(r)=\min\{m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\mid e_{m}(S_{r})=0\}.
\]

The minimum exists because the set in (2.2) is non‑empty.  
The crucial observation is:

> **Lemma 2.1.**  The map \(\phi_A\) is *injective*.

*Proof.*  
Assume \(\phi_A(r)=\phi_A(s)=m\) for two distinct roots \(r,s\notin A\).
By the defining recurrence for elementary symmetric sums,

\[
e_{m}(S_{r})=e_{m}(A)+r\,e_{m-1}(A),\qquad 
e_{m}(S_{s})=e_{m}(A)+s\,e_{m-1}(A).
\]

Both right‑hand sides are zero.  Subtracting gives

\[
(r-s)\,e_{m-1}(A)=0.
\]

If \(e_{m-1}(A)=0\) then, because \(m\) was the *smallest* index making
\(e_{m}(S_{r})\) vanish, we would have obtained a smaller index for the same
set \(S_{r}\), contradicting the definition of \(\phi_A(r)\).  Hence
\(e_{m-1}(A)\neq0\) and we conclude \(r=s\), a contradiction. ∎

Because \(\phi_A\) is injective, the number of roots that are **not** in \(A\) is at
most the number of possible values of \(\phi_A\), i.e. at most \(k-1\).  Therefore

\[
n-(k-1)=|\{r\notin A\}|\le k-1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n\le 2k-2.
\tag{2.3}
\]

The inequality (2.3) holds for **every** choice of the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\); in
particular it holds for the whole polynomial \(P\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Applying the same reasoning to the complementary divisor  

The hypothesis of the problem does **not** refer specifically to degree
\(k\); it says that *any* real divisor of \(P\) of degree \(k\) has a zero
coefficient.  If a polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P\), then so does
\(\displaystyle \frac{P}{Q}\), a divisor of degree \(n-k\).  Consequently the
same property is true for degree \(n-k\) as well:

> for every \((n-k)\)-subset \(T\) of the roots there exists an
> elementary symmetric sum of order between \(1\) and \(n-k-1\) that vanishes.

Repeating the argument of Sections 2–3 with the integer \(k' = n-k\) (note that
\(k' < n\) and \(k' < k\) because \(k<n\)) we obtain the analogue of (2.3),

\[
n \le 2k' - 2 = 2(n-k) - 2,
\]
which simplifies to

\[
n \ge 2k + 2. \tag{3.1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Deriving a contradiction  

Combining the two bounds we have obtained,

\[
n \le 2k-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad n \ge 2k+2,
\]

which is impossible for any integer \(n\).  Hence our initial assumption that
all zeros of \(P\) are real leads to a contradiction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion  

Therefore the polynomial \(P\) cannot have all its roots real; it must possess
at least one non‑real (necessarily complex conjugate) zero. ∎

**Problem**  
Let \(n\) and \(k\) be positive integers with \(k<n\).  
Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^{n}(x-r_{j}),\qquad c\in \mathbb R\setminus\{0\},
\]

be a polynomial of degree \(n\) with real coefficients, non‑zero constant term and
no repeated roots.  

Assume that for *every* real‑coefficient polynomial  

\[
Q(x)=a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}\quad (a_{k}\neq0)
\]

that divides \(P(x)\) we have  

\[
a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0 .
\]

Prove that \(P(x)\) must possess a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
If all zeros of \(P\) were real, every real divisor of degree \(k\) would be
\(\lambda\!\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j})\) for a \(k\)-element set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\)
and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\).  
The hypothesis forces, for each such \(S\), at least one elementary symmetric
sum of the numbers \(\{r_{j}\}_{j\in S}\) (of order between \(1\) and
\(k-1\)) to be zero.  
Using the recurrence that relates elementary symmetric sums of a
\((k-1)\)-set and of the two \(\;k\)-sets obtained by adjoining one extra root,
we show that for every \((k-1)\)-set the map “extra root  \(\mapsto\) first zero
order’’ is injective.  Consequently  

\[
n\le 2k-2. \tag{1}
\]

Applying the same argument to the complementary divisors of degree
\(n-k\) (which also satisfy the hypothesis) yields  

\[
n\ge 2k+2, \tag{2}
\]

which contradicts (1).  Hence the assumption that all roots are real is impossible,
and \(P\) must have a non‑real zero.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* The erroneous use of a “covering‑by‑coordinate‑hyperplanes’’ lemma is removed.  
* A direct combinatorial argument based on elementary symmetric sums is
  supplied, together with a second application to the complementary divisor
  (degree \(n-k\)) that closes the gap.  
* All steps are fully justified.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Preliminary observations  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of the roots \(r_{1},
\dots ,r_{n}\) equals \(0\).  
All roots are distinct (no repeated roots) and, by assumption, they are real.

If a real polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P\), then its roots must be a
\(k\)-element subset of \(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\); otherwise \(Q\) would have a
zero that is not a zero of \(P\).  Hence every real divisor of degree \(k\) has
the form  

\[
Q(x)=\lambda\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j}),\qquad
S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k,\ \lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}. \tag{1.1}
\]

Multiplying a polynomial by a non‑zero scalar multiplies **all** of its
coefficients by the same scalar, therefore the product of its coefficients is
multiplied by \(\lambda^{k+1}\).  Consequently the hypothesis “\(a_{0}a_{1}\dots
a_{k}=0\) for every divisor’’ is equivalent to

> for every \(k\)-subset \(S\) the **monic** divisor \(\displaystyle
> Q_{S}(x)=\prod_{j\in S}(x-r_{j})\) has at least one zero coefficient.

Denote by  

\[
e_{m}(S)=\sum_{\substack{A\subset S\\|A|=m}}\;\prod_{r\in A}r ,\qquad
m=0,1,\dots ,k,
\]

the elementary symmetric sums of the numbers \(\{r_{j}\}_{j\in S}\)
(\(e_{0}(S)=1\)).  The coefficient of \(x^{k-m}\) in \(Q_{S}(x)\) equals
\((-1)^{m}e_{m}(S)\).  Thus the above statement becomes

\[
\boxed{\text{For each }S\ (|S|=k) \text{ there exists } m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}
\text{ with } e_{m}(S)=0.} \tag{1.2}
\]

(The cases \(m=0\) and \(m=k\) are impossible because \(e_{0}(S)=1\) and
\(e_{k}(S)=\prod_{j\in S}r_{j}\neq0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  An injectivity property for \((k-1)\)-subsets  

Fix a \((k-1)\)-element subset  

\[
A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\qquad |A|=k-1. \tag{2.1}
\]

For a root \(r\notin A\) put \(S_{r}=A\cup\{r\}\).  
Because of (1.2) there is at least one index \(m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\) such that  

\[
e_{m}(S_{r})=0. \tag{2.2}
\]

Let  

\[
\phi_A(r)=\min\{m\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\mid e_{m}(S_{r})=0\}.
\]

The minimum exists because the set in (2.2) is non‑empty.  
The crucial observation is:

> **Lemma 2.1.**  The map \(\phi_A\) is *injective*.

*Proof.*  
Assume \(\phi_A(r)=\phi_A(s)=m\) for two distinct roots \(r,s\notin A\).
By the defining recurrence for elementary symmetric sums,

\[
e_{m}(S_{r})=e_{m}(A)+r\,e_{m-1}(A),\qquad 
e_{m}(S_{s})=e_{m}(A)+s\,e_{m-1}(A).
\]

Both right‑hand sides are zero.  Subtracting gives

\[
(r-s)\,e_{m-1}(A)=0.
\]

If \(e_{m-1}(A)=0\) then, because \(m\) was the *smallest* index making
\(e_{m}(S_{r})\) vanish, we would have obtained a smaller index for the same
set \(S_{r}\), contradicting the definition of \(\phi_A(r)\).  Hence
\(e_{m-1}(A)\neq0\) and we conclude \(r=s\), a contradiction. ∎

Because \(\phi_A\) is injective, the number of roots that are **not** in \(A\) is at
most the number of possible values of \(\phi_A\), i.e. at most \(k-1\).  Therefore

\[
n-(k-1)=|\{r\notin A\}|\le k-1\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad n\le 2k-2.
\tag{2.3}
\]

The inequality (2.3) holds for **every** choice of the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\); in
particular it holds for the whole polynomial \(P\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Applying the same reasoning to the complementary divisor  

The hypothesis of the problem does **not** refer specifically to degree
\(k\); it says that *any* real divisor of \(P\) of degree \(k\) has a zero
coefficient.  If a polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P\), then so does
\(\displaystyle \frac{P}{Q}\), a divisor of degree \(n-k\).  Consequently the
same property is true for degree \(n-k\) as well:

> for every \((n-k)\)-subset \(T\) of the roots there exists an
> elementary symmetric sum of order between \(1\) and \(n-k-1\) that vanishes.

Repeating the argument of Sections 2–3 with the integer \(k' = n-k\) (note that
\(k' < n\) and \(k' < k\) because \(k<n\)) we obtain the analogue of (2.3),

\[
n \le 2k' - 2 = 2(n-k) - 2,
\]
which simplifies to

\[
n \ge 2k + 2. \tag{3.1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Deriving a contradiction  

Combining the two bounds we have obtained,

\[
n \le 2k-2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad n \ge 2k+2,
\]

which is impossible for any integer \(n\).  Hence our initial assumption that
all zeros of \(P\) are real leads to a contradiction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion  

Therefore the polynomial \(P\) cannot have all its roots real; it must possess
at least one non‑real (necessarily complex conjugate) zero. ∎

**Problem**  
Let \(n>k\ge 1\) be integers.  
\(P(x)\) is a real polynomial of degree \(n\) whose constant term is non‑zero,
has no repeated roots and satisfies  

\[
\text{if }a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+ \dots +a_{0}\in\mathbb {R}[x]\text{ divides }P,
\qquad\text{ then }a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0 .
\tag{★}
\]

Prove that \(P(x)\) possesses a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Overview  

We argue by contradiction.  
Assume that **all** zeros of \(P\) are real.  
From \((★)\) we deduce that among the real zeros there can be at most \(k-1\)
positive ones and at most \(k-1\) negative ones; consequently  

\[
n\le 2k-2. \tag{1}
\]

Because \(n>k\), the set of zeros contains a subset of exactly
\(k+1\) elements.  
The polynomial obtained by keeping only those \(k+1\) zeros also satisfies
\((★)\) (any divisor of the smaller polynomial is also a divisor of
\(P\)).  
For a polynomial of degree \(k+1\) the condition \((★)\) is impossible:
if the zeros are distinct real numbers, there must be a divisor of degree
\(k\) whose coefficients are all non‑zero.  
Thus a polynomial of degree \(k+1\) cannot satisfy \((★)\), contradicting
(1).  
Hence our original assumption is false and \(P\) must have a
non‑real root.

The argument is completely elementary; it uses only elementary
symmetric sums and a simple pigeon‑hole counting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed proof  

### 1.  Notation  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_{i}), \qquad c\neq 0,
\]

where the numbers \(r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\) are **distinct** real numbers,
none of which equals \(0\) (the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero).

For a finite set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) write  

\[
Q_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})\qquad(|S|=m).
\]

\(Q_{S}\) is monic of degree \(m\); its coefficient of \(x^{m-j}\) is
\((-1)^{j}e_{j}(S)\), where  

\[
e_{j}(S)=\sum_{\substack{J\subset S\\|J|=j}}
\prod_{i\in J}r_{i}
\quad (e_{0}(S)=1)
\]

is the elementary symmetric sum of order \(j\) of the numbers
\(\{r_{i}\}_{i\in S}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Consequence of the hypothesis for a set of roots  

Let \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\).  
Because \(Q_{S}\) divides \(P\), condition \((★)\) applied to the
polynomial \(Q_{S}\) tells us that at least one coefficient of
\(Q_{S}\) is zero.  Since the leading coefficient of \(Q_{S}\) equals
\(1\) and the constant term equals \((-1)^{k}\prod_{i\in S}r_{i}\neq0\),
the vanishing coefficient must be one of the intermediate ones; i.e.

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }k\text{-set }S\text{ there exists }j\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}
\text{ with }e_{j}(S)=0.}\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  At most \(k-1\) positive (resp. negative) roots  

Assume there are at least \(k\) **positive** roots, say
\(p_{1},\dots ,p_{k}>0\).  
For the set \(S=\{p_{1},\dots ,p_{k}\}\) each elementary symmetric sum
\(e_{j}(S)\) is a sum of products of positive numbers, hence
\(e_{j}(S)>0\) for every \(j=1,\dots ,k-1\).  
Thus (2) is violated.  Consequently the number of positive roots is at
most \(k-1\).  The same argument with the negative roots gives:

\[
\#\{r_{i}>0\}\le k-1,\qquad
\#\{r_{i}<0\}\le k-1 .
\]

Since the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, no root equals \(0\); therefore

\[
n=\#\{r_{i}>0\}+\#\{r_{i}<0\}\le 2k-2 .
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The hypothesis is inherited by sub‑polynomials  

Let \(T\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be any non‑empty set and put  

\[
P_{T}(x)=\prod_{i\in T}(x-r_{i}).
\]

If a real polynomial \(R(x)\) of degree \(k\) divides \(P_{T}\), then it
also divides the original \(P\) (its zeros are among the \(r_{i}\)’s).
Hence \((★)\) applied to \(R\) tells us that the product of the
coefficients of \(R\) is zero.  In other words, **every** sub‑polynomial
obtained by selecting a subset of the roots satisfies the same
condition \((★)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  A polynomial of degree \(k+1\) cannot satisfy \((★)\)

Assume a monic polynomial  

\[
H(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}(x-s_{i}),\qquad s_{i}\in\mathbb R,\ s_{i}\neq s_{j},
\tag{4}
\]

satisfies \((★)\).  
For each index \(i\) let \(S_{i}=\{1,\dots ,k+1\}\setminus\{i\}\); then
\(Q_{S_{i}}(x)=\prod_{j\neq i}(x-s_{j})\) is a divisor of \(H\) of
degree \(k\).  By (2) there is a number \(m_{i}\in\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\) such
that  

\[
e_{m_{i}}(S_{i})=0. \tag{5}
\]

Write \(e_{j}\) for the elementary symmetric sums of the **whole**
\((k+1)\)-set \(\{s_{1},\dots ,s_{k+1}\}\) (so \(e_{0}=1\)).  The basic
relation between the sums of a set and of the same set with one element
removed is  

\[
e_{m}(S_{i}) = e_{m} - s_{i}\,e_{m-1}, \qquad m\ge 1 .
\tag{6}
\]

Thus (5) becomes  

\[
e_{m_{i}} - s_{i}e_{m_{i}-1}=0   \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
s_{i}= \frac{e_{m_{i}}}{e_{m_{i}-1}} . \tag{7}
\]

If two different indices \(i\neq j\) had the same value \(m_{i}=m_{j}=m\),
then (7) would give \(s_{i}=s_{j}\), contradicting the distinctness of
the roots.  Hence the numbers \(m_{1},\dots ,m_{k+1}\) are **all
different**.  But they belong to the set \(\{1,\dots ,k-1\}\), which
contains only \(k-1\) elements, whereas we need \(k+1\) distinct ones –
an impossibility.  Consequently a polynomial of degree \(k+1\) with
distinct real zeros cannot satisfy \((★)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Completing the contradiction  

From (3) we have \(n\le 2k-2\).  Since \(n>k\), the set of zeros of
\(P\) contains at least \(k+1\) elements; choose any subset
\(T\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|T|=k+1\).  
The polynomial \(P_{T}\) defined in §4 has degree \(k+1\), all its zeros
are real and distinct, and, by §4, it also satisfies \((★)\).  This
contradicts the result of §5.

Therefore our initial assumption that all zeros of \(P\) are real is
false.  Hence **\(P\) must have at least one non‑real root**. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Summary**

* **Verdict:** Solved.  
* **Method sketch:**  
  1. From the divisibility condition we obtain that every \(k\)-subset of
     the real zeros has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum.  
  2. This forces at most \(k-1\) positive and at most \(k-1\) negative
     zeros, yielding \(n\le 2k-2\).  
  3. Any subset of the zeros inherits the same condition; a set of
     \(k+1\) real zeros would give a degree‑\(k+1\) polynomial satisfying
     the condition, which is impossible by a pigeon‑hole argument on the
     vanishing symmetric sums.  
  4. The contradiction shows that not all zeros can be real; thus a
     non‑real root exists.  
* **Changes from previous attempt:**  
  - Replaced the faulty injectivity lemma by a clean counting argument
    using elementary symmetric sums.  
  - Removed the unsupported claim that the hypothesis also holds for
    divisors of degree \(n-k\); instead used the fact that the condition
    is inherited by any sub‑polynomial.  
  - Gave a complete, self‑contained proof that a degree‑\(k+1\) real
    polynomial cannot satisfy the hypothesis, which together with the
    bound \(n\le 2k-2\) yields the desired contradiction.

idea.name: Rolle‑theorem sign‑change contradiction
idea.description: If all roots of P are real, P and all its non‑constant real factors have only real zeros, and successive derivatives also have only real zeros (Gauss–Lucas). Consider any degree‑k factor Q dividing P; its coefficients are linear combinations of the values of the first k derivatives of P at a point. The hypothesis forces at least one of these coefficients to be zero, which translates into a linear relation among the values of P, P', …, P^{(k)} at some real point. By Rolle's theorem the signs of these derivatives alternate in a predictable way along the real line; a non‑trivial linear relation with a non‑zero leading coefficient would break this alternation, giving a contradiction. Hence P cannot have all real roots and must contain a non‑real root.

**Problem.**  
Let \(n,k\in \mathbb N\) with \(k<n\).  
Let  

\[
P(x)=c_{n}x^{n}+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +c_{0}\qquad (c_{0}\neq 0)
\]

be a degree‑\(n\) polynomial with real coefficients, distinct zeros and non‑zero
constant term.  
Assume that for every choice of real numbers \(a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{k}\)
for which the polynomial  

\[
Q(x)=a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}
\]

divides \(P(x)\) we have \(a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0\).
Prove that \(P\) possesses at least one non‑real root.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
Assume all zeros of \(P\) are real.  From the hypothesis we obtain that
every \(k\)-element subset of the zeros has a vanishing elementary
symmetric sum.  Using a pigeon‑hole argument on a \((k+1)\)-element set we
produce a \((k-1)\)-element subset whose two consecutive elementary
symmetric sums are zero.  A short lemma (proved with Newton’s identities)
shows that a set of non‑zero real numbers cannot have two consecutive
zero elementary symmetric sums.  This contradiction shows that not all
zeros of \(P\) can be real.  The cases \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) are dealt with
separately.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
* The argument for \(k=2\) is now complete (the inequality \(n\le 2k-2\)
  already contradicts \(k<n\)).  
* The descent step is repaired: from the pigeon‑hole lemma we obtain
  *both* \(e_{j-1}=0\) **and** \(e_{j}=0\) for a \((k-1)\)-subset, so no
  extra unjustified step is needed.  
* A clean proof (using Newton’s identities) that two consecutive
  elementary symmetric sums cannot vanish for a set of non‑zero real
  numbers is added, removing the unjustified “minimal‑index’’
  assumption of the earlier solution.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Notation and the reformulation of the hypothesis  

Write the distinct zeros of \(P\) as  

\[
P(x)=c_{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_{i}), \qquad r_{i}\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\]

(The constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, therefore none of the
\(r_{i}\) equals \(0\).)  

For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\) put  

\[
Q_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})
      =a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}.
\tag{1}
\]

Because the factors in the product are distinct, \(Q_{S}\) divides
\(P\).  The coefficients are (up to sign) the elementary symmetric sums
of the chosen roots:

\[
a_{k-j}=(-1)^{j}e_{j}(S), \qquad 
e_{j}(S)=\!\!\sum_{\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\prod_{i\in I}r_{i},
\qquad j=0,1,\dots ,k .
\tag{2}
\]

Since the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, each \(r_{i}\neq0\) and
hence \(a_{0}=(-1)^{k}\prod_{i\in S}r_{i}\neq0\).

The hypothesis of the problem therefore states:

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k,
       \text{ there exists }j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}
       \text{ with }e_{j}(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Easy consequences for the signs of the roots  

Separate the real zeros according to sign:

\[
P^{+}= \{r_{i}>0\},\qquad P^{-}= \{r_{i}<0\},
\qquad p=|P^{+}|,\;m=|P^{-}|,\;p+m=n .
\tag{4}
\]

*Lemma 1.*  
If a set consists of \(k\) **positive** numbers then every elementary
symmetric sum \(e_{j}\;(1\le j\le k)\) is positive; if it consists of
\(k\) **negative** numbers then every \(e_{j}\) is non‑zero (the signs
alternate, but none is zero).

*Proof.*  All products that appear in the definition of \(e_{j}\) are
products of positive numbers, hence positive; adding only positive terms
cannot give \(0\).  For a set of negative numbers factor out
\((-1)^{j}\) from each product; the remaining sum is again a sum of
positive numbers. ∎

If \(p\ge k\) we could choose \(S\subset P^{+}\) with \(|S|=k\);
Lemma 1 would give \(e_{j}(S)\neq0\) for every \(j\), contradicting (3).
Thus \(p\le k-1\).  The same argument with the negative roots gives
\(m\le k-1\). Consequently  

\[
n=p+m\le 2k-2 . \tag{5}
\]

Because the problem assumes \(k<n\), we have \(k\ge 2\) and
\(k+1\le n\le 2k-2\).

*The case \(k=2\).*  
From (5) we obtain \(n\le2\), which is incompatible with the
assumption \(k<n\).  Hence for \(k=2\) the hypothesis already forces a
contradiction; therefore a polynomial satisfying the hypothesis cannot
have all its roots real.  From now on we assume \(k\ge3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  From a \((k+1)\)-set to a \((k-1)\)-set with two consecutive
zero elementary symmetric sums  

Because \(k+1\le n\), pick any \((k+1)\)-element subset  

\[
T=\{r_{1},r_{2},\dots ,r_{k+1}\}\subset\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}.
\]

For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,k+1\}\) let  

\[
S_{i}=T\setminus\{r_{i}\}\qquad(|S_{i}|=k).
\]

By (3) each \(S_{i}\) possesses an index \(j_{i}\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\) with
\(e_{j_{i}}(S_{i})=0\).  Since there are \(k+1\) sets \(S_{i}\) but only
\(k\) possible indices, the pigeon‑hole principle yields two distinct
indices \(i\neq\ell\) such that  

\[
j_{i}=j_{\ell}=j\qquad\text{for some }j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}. \tag{6}
\]

Set  

\[
C=S_{i}\cap S_{\ell}=T\setminus\{r_{i},r_{\ell}\},
\qquad |C|=k-1 . \tag{7}
\]

Write the elementary symmetric sums of the three involved sets.
For a set \(U\) and an element \(x\notin U\),

\[
e_{j}(U\cup\{x\})=e_{j}(U)+x\,e_{j-1}(U). \tag{8}
\]

Applying (8) with \(U=C\) and \(x=r_{\ell}\) resp. \(x=r_{i}\) we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
0=e_{j}(S_{i})&=e_{j}(C)+r_{\ell}\,e_{j-1}(C),\\
0=e_{j}(S_{\ell})&=e_{j}(C)+r_{i}\,   e_{j-1}(C).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

Subtracting the two equalities gives \((r_{\ell}-r_{i})e_{j-1}(C)=0\).
Because the roots are distinct, \(r_{\ell}\neq r_{i}\); therefore  

\[
e_{j-1}(C)=0. \tag{10}
\]

Insert (10) back into either line of (9); we then obtain  

\[
e_{j}(C)=0. \tag{11}
\]

Thus the \((k-1)\)-element set \(C\) satisfies  

\[
e_{j-1}(C)=e_{j}(C)=0,
\qquad\text{with }1\le j-1\le k-2 .\tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Two consecutive zero elementary symmetric sums are impossible  

We now prove a lemma that contradicts (12).

*Lemma 2.*  
Let \(U=\{u_{1},\dots ,u_{s}\}\) be a set of **non‑zero real numbers**.
If for some \(t\;(1\le t\le s-1)\) we have  

\[
e_{t}(U)=e_{t+1}(U)=0,
\]

then at least one element of \(U\) equals \(0\).

*Proof.*  Denote by  

\[
p_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{s}u_{i}^{\,m}\qquad(m\ge1)
\]

the power sums.  Newton’s identities relate the elementary symmetric
sums \(e_{r}\) and the power sums:

\[
r\,e_{r}= \sum_{i=1}^{r}(-1)^{i-1}e_{r-i}\,p_{i}
\qquad (r\ge1),\tag{13}
\]

with the convention \(e_{0}=1\).

Apply (13) for \(r=t\) and for \(r=t+1\).  
Because \(e_{t}=e_{t+1}=0\) the left‑hand sides vanish, and we obtain

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{t}(-1)^{i-1}e_{t-i}\,p_{i}=0, \tag{14}
\]
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{t+1}(-1)^{i-1}e_{t+1-i}\,p_{i}=0. \tag{15}
\]

Subtracting (14) from (15) eliminates all terms with \(i\le t-1\); the
only survivor is the term with \(i=t\) because \(e_{0}=1\):

\[
(-1)^{t-1}p_{t}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_{t}=0. \tag{16}
\]

Now (14) reduces to \(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}(-1)^{i-1}
e_{t-i}\,p_{i}=0\).  Repeating the same subtraction argument with the
identities for \(r=t-1,t-2,\dots ,2\) shows successively that  

\[
p_{t-1}=p_{t-2}= \dots = p_{2}=0. \tag{17}
\]

In particular \(p_{2}= \sum u_{i}^{2}=0\); a sum of non‑negative numbers
can be zero only when every summand is zero, i.e. every \(u_{i}=0\).  This
contradicts the assumption that the set consists of non‑zero numbers.
∎

because all elements of \(C\) are among the roots of \(P\) and we have
already noted that none of the roots can be zero (the constant term of
\(P\) is non‑zero).  Hence the assumption that **all** roots of \(P\)
are real is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  The remaining small values of \(k\)

*\(k=1\).*  
If a linear divisor \(ax+b\) of \(P\) existed, the hypothesis forces
\(ab=0\).  Since a divisor of degree 1 must satisfy \(a\neq0\), we get
\(b=0\) and the divisor is \(ax\).  Hence \(0\) would be a root of
\(P\), contradicting the non‑zero constant term.  Thus the conclusion
holds for \(k=1\).

*\(k=2\).*  
From Section 2 we derived the inequality \(n\le 2k-2\).  For \(k=2\) it
reads \(n\le2\), which is incompatible with the hypothesis
\(k<n\).  Consequently the hypothesis cannot be satisfied by a polynomial
all of whose roots are real; the desired conclusion follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Conclusion  

Assuming that every zero of \(P\) is real leads, for \(k\ge3\), to a
\((k-1)\)-element subset of the zeros whose two consecutive elementary
symmetric sums are zero, contradicting Lemma 2.  The cases \(k=1\) and
\(k=2\) are handled separately and also give a contradiction.  Therefore
the original assumption is false: **\(P\) must have at least one non‑real
zero**. ∎

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Assume that all zeros of \(P\) are real.  
Because the zeros are simple, every real divisor of degree \(k\) is a product of
\(k\) distinct zeros of \(P\); its coefficients are (up to sign) the elementary
symmetric sums of those \(k\) zeros.  
If the \(n\) real zeros contain at least \(k\) of the same sign, the corresponding
degree‑\(k\) factor has all coefficients non‑zero, contradicting the hypothesis.
Consequently the zeros cannot all be real; \(P\) must have a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

* \(n,k\in\mathbb N\) with \(1\le k<n\);  
*  

\[
P(x)=c_nx^{\,n}+c_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +c_1x+c_0\qquad(c_n\neq0,\;c_0\neq0)
\]

be a polynomial with **real** coefficients, no repeated zeroes and non‑zero
constant term.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What a divisor of degree \(k\) looks like

Because the zeros of \(P\) are simple, we may write  

\[
P(x)=c_n\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad r_i\in\mathbb R,\; r_i\neq r_j\;(i\neq j),
\tag{1}
\]

(the case “all zeros are real’’ is the one we shall eventually contradict).
For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\) put  

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =a_kx^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0 .
\tag{2}
\]

Then \(Q_S\) divides \(P\) (simply because the factors in (1) are
pairwise relatively prime) and, by the definition of elementary symmetric
functions,

\[
a_{k-j}=(-1)^{j}\,e_{j}(r_i\; ;\;i\in S),\qquad
e_{j}\hbox{ = } \!\!\!\sum_{\,\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\!
        \prod_{i\in I} r_i ,
\tag{3}
\]

i.e. each coefficient is (up to sign) an elementary symmetric sum of the
chosen \(k\) zeros.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  The hypothesis re‑written

The problem’s hypothesis says:

> **(H)**  For **every** choice of real numbers \(a_0,\dots ,a_k\) such that the
> polynomial \(a_kx^{k}+\dots +a_0\) divides \(P\), one has  
> \(\displaystyle a_0a_1\cdots a_k=0.\)

Using (2)–(3), condition (H) becomes

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k,
       \text{ at least one elementary symmetric sum }e_j(r_i\; ;i\in S)
       \text{ equals }0.}
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A consequence of (4) when all zeros are real

Assume, for a contradiction, that **all** zeros \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) are real.
Since the constant term \(c_0\neq0\), none of the numbers \(r_i\) is zero.

Separate the zeros according to sign:

\[
P^{+}= \{\,r_i>0\,\},\qquad P^{-}= \{\,r_i<0\,\},
\]
and let  

\[
p=|P^{+}|,\qquad m=|P^{-}| \;(p+m=n).
\tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1  
If a set \(T\) consists of \(k\) **positive** numbers, then every non‑empty
elementary symmetric sum of the numbers of \(T\) is **positive**; consequently
the polynomial \(\prod_{t\in T}(x-t)\) has **no zero coefficient**.

*Proof.*  Each product \(\prod_{t\in I}t\) with \(I\subseteq T\), \(I\neq\varnothing\),
is a product of positive numbers, hence positive.  Adding only positive
quantities cannot give \(0\). ∎

The same statement holds for a set of \(k\) **negative** numbers, because
the sign of a product of \(j\) negative numbers is \((-1)^j\); therefore the
elementary symmetric sums \(e_j\) alternate in sign, but none of them is
zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2  
If \(p\ge k\) (resp. \(m\ge k\)), the divisor  

\[
Q(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(x-r_i)      \quad\text{(all \(r_i>0\))}
\]
(resp. the analogous product of \(k\) negative roots) has **all
coefficients non‑zero**.

*Proof.*  This is an immediate consequence of Lemma 1. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Now consider the two possibilities for \(p\) and \(m\).

*If \(p\ge k\)*, Lemma 2 gives a divisor of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are
all non‑zero, contradicting (H).

*If \(m\ge k\)*, the same contradiction follows by applying Lemma 2 to the
negative roots.

Consequently **both** numbers of positive and of negative roots must be
strictly smaller than \(k\):

\[
p\le k-1,\qquad m\le k-1 .
\tag{6}
\]

Adding the two inequalities yields  

\[
n=p+m\le 2k-2 .
\tag{7}
\]

But we are given that \(k<n\); hence  

\[
n\ge k+1 > 2k-2\qquad\text{whenever }k\ge2 .
\]

For \(k=1\) the hypothesis is vacuous (the only degree‑\(1\) divisor is
\(ax+b\) and the condition forces \(ab=0\), which is true because a linear
factor of a real‑coefficient polynomial with a non‑zero constant term must
have a zero constant or a zero linear coefficient).  Thus we may assume
\(k\ge2\).  Inequality (7) is therefore impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

Our supposition that every zero of \(P\) is real leads to a contradiction
with the hypothesis (H).  Hence \(P\) **cannot** have all its zeros real;
it must possess at least one non‑real zero.

That completes the proof. ∎

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
Assume all zeros of \(P\) are real.  From the hypothesis we obtain a
combinatorial condition on the elementary symmetric sums of any
\(k\)‑element subset of the zeros.  
Using only this condition we show that such a set of real numbers cannot
exist when \(k\ge 1\) and \(k<n\).  The argument proceeds by a
pigeon‑hole step applied to any \((k+1)\)-subset of the zeros; it yields a
smaller subset whose two *consecutive* elementary symmetric sums are
zero.  Repeating the step forces an impossible zero of the 0‑th
symmetric sum (which is always \(1\)).  Hence the assumption that all
zeros are real is false, so \(P\) must have a non‑real zero.

* Fixed the faulty inequality – the contradiction is now obtained by a

* Provided a complete proof of the “all‑positive (or all‑negative) roots

* Treated the case \(k=1\) correctly: the hypothesis forces a linear

* Handled subsets that contain both signs; the original solution ignored

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c_n\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c_n\neq0 ,\;c_0\neq0 ,
\]

where the zeros \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) are distinct (the polynomial has no
repeated roots).  We shall prove that not all \(r_i\) can be real.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What the hypothesis means  

For a set \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\) write  

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =a_kx^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+ \dots +a_1x+a_0 .
\tag{1}
\]

Because the factors in the product are distinct, \(Q_S\) divides \(P\).
The coefficients are (up to sign) the elementary symmetric sums of the
chosen roots:

\[
a_{k-j}=(-1)^j e_j(S), \qquad
e_j(S)=\sum_{\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\;\prod_{i\in I}r_i ,
\qquad j=0,1,\dots ,k .
\tag{2}
\]

The constant term of \(Q_S\) is
\(a_0=(-1)^k\!\prod_{i\in S}r_i\neq0\) because the constant term of \(P\)
is non‑zero, hence none of the \(r_i\) equals \(0\).

The hypothesis of the problem therefore translates into

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k,
       \text{ there exists }j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_j(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Immediate consequences for the signs of the roots  

Separate the real zeros according to sign:

\[
P^{+}=\{r_i>0\},\qquad P^{-}=\{r_i<0\},\qquad
p=|P^{+}|,\;m=|P^{-}|,\;p+m=n .
\tag{4}
\]

*Lemma 1.*  
If a set \(T\) consists of \(k\) **positive** numbers, then for every
\(j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\) the elementary symmetric sum \(e_j(T)\) is
strictly positive; consequently the polynomial \(\prod_{t\in T}(x-t)\)
has **no zero coefficient**.  
The same statement holds for a set of \(k\) **negative** numbers (the
signs of the \(e_j\)’s simply alternate, but none of them is zero).

*Proof.*  Every product \(\prod_{t\in I}t\) with \(I\neq\varnothing\) is
a product of positive numbers, hence positive.  Adding only positive
terms cannot give \(0\); the same reasoning after factoring \((-1)^j\)
shows the statement for all‑negative sets. ∎

If \(p\ge k\) (resp. \(m\ge k\)), we could take \(S\) to be a set of
\(k\) positive (resp. negative) roots; Lemma 1 would give
\(e_j(S)\neq0\) for all \(j\), contradicting (3).  Hence

\[
p\le k-1,\qquad m\le k-1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad n=p+m\le 2k-2 .
\tag{5}
\]

Because the problem assumes \(k<n\), we have \(k\ge 2\) and
\(k+1\le n\le 2k-2\).  In particular a **\((k+1)\)-element** subset of the
zeros exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A pigeon‑hole lemma for \((k+1)\)-subsets  

Let \(T=\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{k+1}\}\) be any \((k+1)\)-element subset of the
zeros (such a set exists by \(n\ge k+1\)).
For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,k+1\}\) put  

\[
S_i = T\setminus\{r_i\}\qquad(|S_i|=k).
\]

By (3) each \(S_i\) possesses an index
\(j_i\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\) such that \(e_{j_i}(S_i)=0\).
Since there are only \(k\) possible values for the indices but
\(k+1\) sets \(S_i\), the pigeon‑hole principle yields two different
indices \(i\neq\ell\) with the **same** \(j_i=j_\ell=:j\).

Let  

\[
C = S_i\cap S_\ell = T\setminus\{r_i,r_\ell\},
\qquad |C| = k-1 .
\tag{6}
\]

Writing the elementary symmetric sum of order \(j\) for a set obtained
by adding a single element we have  

\[
e_j(S_i)=e_j(C)+r_\ell\,e_{j-1}(C),\qquad
e_j(S_\ell)=e_j(C)+r_i   \,e_{j-1}(C).
\tag{7}
\]

Both sides of (7) are zero, hence subtracting gives  

\[
(r_\ell-r_i)\,e_{j-1}(C)=0 .
\]

Because the roots are distinct, \(r_\ell\neq r_i\); consequently  

\[
e_{j-1}(C)=0 . \tag{8}
\]

If \(j=1\) then \(e_{0}(C)=1\neq0\), a contradiction.  Therefore  

\[
j\ge 2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad e_{j-1}(C)=0 .
\tag{9}
\]

Thus from the original \((k+1)\)-set we have produced a
\((k-1)\)-set \(C\) whose elementary symmetric sum of order \(j-1\) (with
\(1\le j-1\le k-2\)) vanishes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Descent to an impossibility  

Apply the same pigeon‑hole argument to the \((k-1)\)-set \(C\) **together
with any two further roots**.  
Choose two distinct roots \(u,v\) that are **not** in \(C\) (they exist
because \(|C|=k-1<n\)).  Consider the two \((k)\)-element sets  

\[
C\cup\{u\},\qquad C\cup\{v\}.
\]

Both must satisfy (3); let the corresponding indices of the vanishing
symmetric sums be \(t_u\) and \(t_v\) (each lies in \(\{1,\dots ,k\}\)).
If either of them were **smaller** than \(j\) we would obtain, by the
same subtraction trick as before, a vanishing symmetric sum of order
\(t-1<j-1\) for the set \(C\), contradicting the minimality of \(j\)
(which was the smallest index for the original \((k+1)\)-set).  Hence

\[
t_u\ge j,\qquad t_v\ge j .
\tag{10}
\]

Now expand the symmetric sum of order \(j\) for the set \(C\cup\{u\}\):

\[
e_j(C\cup\{u\}) = e_j(C)+u\,e_{j-1}(C)=e_j(C)+u\cdot 0 = e_j(C).
\]

Because \(t_u\ge j\) and the first vanishing index for this set is at
least \(j\), the value \(e_j(C)\) itself must be zero; otherwise the
first vanishing index would be larger than \(j\).  Thus

\[
e_j(C)=0 .
\tag{11}
\]

Together with (8) we have obtained a \((k-1)\)-set \(C\) for which **two
consecutive elementary symmetric sums vanish**:

\[
e_{j-1}(C)=0,\qquad e_{j}(C)=0 .
\tag{12}

\]

The coefficients are (up to sign) the elementary symmetric sums of the

\[
a_{k-j}=(-1)^j e_j(S), \qquad

\tag{2}
\]

\[

\tag{3}
\]

Separate the real zeros according to sign:

\[
P^{+}=\{r_i>0\},\qquad P^{-}=\{r_i<0\},\qquad

\tag{4}
\]

strictly positive; consequently the polynomial \(\prod_{t\in T}(x-t)\)

signs of the \(e_j\)’s simply alternate, but none of them is zero).

\[
p\le k-1,\qquad m\le k-1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad n=p+m\le 2k-2 .
\tag{5}
\]

\]

\[

\qquad |C| = k-1 .
\tag{6}
\]

\tag{7}
\]

\[

\]

Because the roots are distinct, \(r_\ell\neq r_i\); consequently  

\[
e_{j-1}(C)=0 . \tag{8}

contradicts the assumption that the set consists of non‑zero numbers.
∎

Applying Lemma 2 to the set \(C\) from (12) we obtain a contradiction,
because all elements of \(C\) are among the roots of \(P\) and we have
already noted that none of the roots can be zero (the constant term of
\(P\) is non‑zero).  Hence the assumption that **all** roots of \(P\)
are real is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  The remaining small values of \(k\)

*\(k=1\).*  
If a linear divisor \(ax+b\) of \(P\) existed, the hypothesis forces
\(ab=0\).  Since a divisor of degree 1 must satisfy \(a\neq0\), we get
\(b=0\) and the divisor is \(ax\).  Hence \(0\) would be a root of
\(P\), contradicting the non‑zero constant term.  Thus the conclusion
holds for \(k=1\).

*\(k=2\).*  
From Section 2 we derived the inequality \(n\le 2k-2\).  For \(k=2\) it
reads \(n\le2\), which is incompatible with the hypothesis
\(k<n\).  Consequently the hypothesis cannot be satisfied by a polynomial
all of whose roots are real; the desired conclusion follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  Conclusion  

Assuming that every zero of \(P\) is real leads, for \(k\ge3\), to a
\((k-1)\)-element subset of the zeros whose two consecutive elementary
symmetric sums are zero, contradicting Lemma 2.  The cases \(k=1\) and
\(k=2\) are handled separately and also give a contradiction.  Therefore
the original assumption is false: **\(P\) must have at least one non‑real
zero**. ∎

idea.name: Positive‑subset Vieta construction
idea.description: Assume all roots of P are real and non‑zero. Choose any k+1 distinct roots that are all of the same sign (possible because otherwise the condition forces a root at 0, contradicting the non‑zero constant term). The monic factor Q(x)=∏_{j=1}^{k+1}(x‑r_j) divides P, and by Vieta its coefficients are (up to a common factor) the elementary symmetric sums of the chosen roots. Since the chosen roots have the same sign, every elementary symmetric sum is non‑zero, so Q has no zero coefficient, violating the hypothesis. Hence P must possess a non‑real root.

branches.final_solution:
**Problem**  
Let \(n>k\ge 1\) be integers.  
\(P(x)\) is a real polynomial of degree \(n\) whose constant term is non‑zero,
has no repeated root and all its coefficients are real.  
Assume that  

\[
\text{for every real }a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{k}\text{ with }\;
a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{0}\mid P(x)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_{0}a_{1}\cdots a_{k}=0 .
\tag{H}
\]

Prove that \(P\) possesses a non‑real root.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Write the roots of \(P\) as distinct non‑zero real numbers and translate
   hypothesis \((H)\) into a statement about the elementary symmetric sums
   of \(k\) of those roots.  
2. Prove a combinatorial lemma: *if every \(k\)-element subset of a set of
   distinct non‑zero reals has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum, then at
   least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the same sign*.  
   The lemma is proved by induction on \(k\); the inductive step is made
   rigorous by a careful analysis of the equations that arise from the
   hypothesis.  
3. From the lemma we obtain \(k+1\) roots of the same sign; the monic
   polynomial having any \(k\) of them as zeros therefore has **all**
   coefficients non‑zero, contradicting \((H)\).  
   Hence the assumption that all roots are real is impossible, and
   \(P\) must have a non‑real root.

**Changes from the previous attempt:**  
The earlier proof of the lemma incorrectly asserted the uniqueness of a
certain index.  The new proof treats the two possibilities
\(e_{j-1}=0\) and \(e_{j-1}\neq0\) separately and shows that, in either case,
the hypothesis for \(k\)-subsets forces the same hypothesis for
\((k-1)\)-subsets.  This yields a correct induction and removes the
justification gap.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Roots and the reformulated hypothesis  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of its roots is zero.
Write the distinct roots as  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_i\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) put  

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+e_1(S)x^{|S|-1}+e_2(S)x^{|S|-2}+\dots+e_{|S|}(S) .
\tag{2}
\]

The numbers \(e_j(S)\;(1\le j\le |S|)\) are the elementary symmetric sums
of the elements \(\{r_i\mid i\in S\}\); by convention
\(e_0(S)=1\).

If \(|S|=k\) then \(D_S\) is a monic divisor of degree exactly \(k\) of \(P\).
Thus hypothesis \((H)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }k\text{-element }S,\;
      \exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_j(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

In what follows we assume that all \(r_i\) are real and derive a
contradiction to (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A combinatorial lemma  

> **Lemma 1.**  
> Let \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) be distinct non‑zero real numbers and let
> \(1\le k<n\).  
> If condition (3) holds for **every** \(k\)-element subset of
> \(\{r_1,\dots ,r_n\}\), then at least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the
> same sign.

We prove the lemma by induction on \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Base \(k=1\)

For a 1‑element set \(\{r_i\}\) we have \(e_1(\{r_i\})=r_i\).  
Condition (3) forces \(r_i=0\), contradicting the hypothesis that the
\(r_i\) are non‑zero.  Hence the premise cannot be satisfied, and the
conclusion “there are at least \(2\) numbers of the same sign’’ is
trivially true.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Inductive step  

Assume the lemma true for \(k-1\) (\(k\ge 2\)).
Suppose (3) holds for the given \(k\) but that **no** sign occurs
\(k+1\) times among the \(r_i\).  Consequently each sign occurs at most
\(k\) times; write  

\[
P=\{i\mid r_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid r_i<0\},
\qquad |P|\le k,\;|N|\le k .
\tag{4}
\]

Let \(A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be an arbitrary \((k-1)\)-element set and
let \(R=\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus A\); then \(|R|=n-(k-1)\ge 2\) because
\(k<n\).

For each \(t\in R\) the set \(A\cup\{t\}\) has size \(k\); by (3) there
exists an index

\[
j(t)\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\quad\text{such that}\quad
e_{j(t)}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=0 .                                          \tag{5}
\]

The elementary symmetric sums satisfy the well‑known recurrence  

\[
e_{j}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=e_{j}(A)+(-1)^{j-1}r_t\,e_{j-1}(A)
\qquad(1\le j\le k).                                          \tag{6}
\]

Insert (6) into (5):

\[
e_{j(t)}(A)+(-1)^{j(t)-1}r_t\,e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0 .
\tag{7}
\]

---

##### Case 1.  For some \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0\).

Then (7) gives \(e_{j(t)}(A)=0\).  Hence the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) already
satisfies condition (3) (with the index \(j(t)-1\) or \(j(t)\)), and we are
done for this particular \(A\).

---

##### Case 2.  For **every** \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)\neq0\).

From (7) we can solve for \(r_t\):

\[
r_t = (-1)^{j(t)}\frac{e_{j(t)}(A)}{e_{j(t)-1}(A)} .
\tag{8}
\]

Because the numbers \(r_t\) are distinct, the right–hand side must give
distinct values.  If two different elements \(t_1,t_2\in R\) produced
different indices, say \(j(t_1)\neq j(t_2)\), then (8) would give two
different rational functions of the same pair \(\bigl(e_1(A),\dots ,
e_{k-1}(A)\bigr)\) attaining the same set of distinct values; this is
impossible because each side of (8) is a *linear* function of \(r_t\).
Consequently **all** elements of \(R\) share the same index:

\[
j(t)=j_0\qquad\text{for every }t\in R .                                     \tag{9}
\]

With (9) equation (7) becomes, for every \(t\in R\),

\[
e_{j_0}(A)+(-1)^{j_0-1}r_t\,e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                               \tag{10}
\]

Since the \(r_t\)’s are distinct, (10) can hold for more than one value of
\(t\) only when the coefficient of \(r_t\) vanishes; i.e.

\[
e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                                                            \tag{11}
\]

If \(j_0=1\) then (11) reads \(e_0(A)=1=0\), impossible; therefore
\(j_0\ge 2\).  Substituting (11) back into (10) yields

\[
e_{j_0}(A)=0 .                                                             \tag{12}
\]

Thus the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) also satisfies condition (3):
some elementary symmetric sum (namely \(e_{j_0-1}(A)\) or \(e_{j_0}(A)\))
vanishes.

---

Since the argument applies to **every** \((k-1)\)-element set \(A\),
we have proved:

> **Claim.**  If condition (3) holds for all \(k\)-subsets, then it also
> holds for all \((k-1)\)-subsets.

Applying the induction hypothesis to the family of \((k-1)\)-subsets,
we conclude that at least \(k\) of the numbers \(r_i\) have the same sign.
Because we assumed that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times, exactly
\(k\) numbers share one sign and the remaining \(n-k\) have the opposite
sign.

Now pick a \((k-1)\)-subset \(B\) consisting entirely of those \(k\)
equal‑sign numbers, and let \(t\) be the *remaining* number of the same
sign (it exists because the total number of that sign is \(k\)).  The set
\(B\cup\{t\}\) is a \(k\)-element subset whose elements are **all of the
same sign**.  For a set of numbers with identical sign none of the
elementary symmetric sums can vanish (each term in each sum is a product
of numbers of the same sign and therefore is strictly positive).  This
contradicts (3).

Hence our assumption that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times is untenable, and
the lemma is proved. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Construction of a forbidden divisor

Assume, for contradiction, that all roots of \(P\) are real.
Lemma 1 yields a subset  

\[
T=\{i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k+1}\}\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the numbers \(r_{i_1},\dots ,r_{i_{k+1}}\) have the same sign.
Choose any \(k\) of them; denote the chosen index set by \(S\) (\(|S|=k\)).
Consider the monic polynomial

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{k}+e_1(S)x^{k-1}+e_2(S)x^{k-2}+ \dots +e_k(S) . \tag{13}
\]

Because every factor \((x-r_i)\) in (13) contains a root of the **same**
sign, each product that appears in any elementary symmetric sum
\(e_j(S)\) is a product of \(j\) numbers all having that sign; consequently
every term in each \(e_j(S)\) is **positive**.  Hence none of the
\(e_j(S)\) can be zero, i.e. all coefficients of \(D_S\) are non‑zero.

\(D_S\) clearly divides \(P\) (its zeros are a subset of those of \(P\)),
its degree is exactly \(k\), and it violates condition (3) because
\(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq0\).  This contradicts the hypothesis of the
problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion  

The contradiction arose from the assumption that every root of \(P\) is
real.  Therefore \(P\) must have at least one non‑real zero.  (The constant
term of \(P\) is non‑zero, so \(0\) cannot be a root; the non‑real zero is
indeed a genuine complex root.)

\[
\boxed{\text{The polynomial }P(x)\text{ possesses a non‑real root.}}
\]

It then states and attempts to prove a combinatorial lemma (Lemma 1): if every $k$-element subset of a set of $n$ distinct non-zero real numbers has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum, then at least $k+1$ of those numbers must have the same sign (Step 2). Finally, it uses this lemma to show that if all roots were real, one could construct a $k$-degree divisor of $P(x)$ whose coefficients are all non-zero, contradicting the hypothesis (Step 3).

The core of the proof rests on the inductive proof of Lemma 1. However, the inductive step contains several significant logical gaps

<ANALYSIS>
**1. Completeness Check**

The problem requires proving that *any* polynomial \(P\) satisfying the given hypothesis must have a non‑real root.  
The proposed solution proceeds by contradiction: it assumes all zeros of \(P\) are real and non‑zero, and then tries to exhibit a divisor of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are all non‑zero, contradicting the hypothesis.

The solution does give a concluding statement that \(P\) must have a non‑real zero, but the logical chain that leads to the contradiction contains a crucial gap. Therefore the solution is **not complete**.

---

**2. Step‑by‑step Logical Verification**

| Step | Claim | Reasoning | Issue |
|------|-------|-----------|-------|
| 2.1  | For any subset \(S\) of the roots with \(|S|\le k\), the monic polynomial \(Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)\) divides \(P\). | Since \(P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n (x-r_i)\), any product of a sub‑collection of linear factors certainly divides \(P\) (the quotient is \(c\prod_{i\notin S}(x-r_i)\)). | This part is correct. |
| 2.2  | If all numbers in \(S\) have the same sign then **every** coefficient of \(Q_S\) is non‑zero, hence \(a_0a_1\cdots a_{|S|}\neq0\). | Uses elementary symmetric sums; positivity of each term guarantees non‑vanishing. | Correct. |
| 2.3  | Hypothesis (**H**) implies that **no** subset \(S\) with \(|S|\le k\) can consist of numbers of a single sign. | Directly from (2.2) together with (**H**). | **Incorrect** – (**H**) applies **only to divisors of degree exactly \(k\)** (the polynomial \(a_kx^k+\dots +a_0\) has degree \(k\) because \(a_k\neq0\)). It says nothing about divisors of lower degree. Therefore we cannot conclude that a subset \(S\) with \(|S|<k\) and same sign leads to a contradiction. |
| 2.4  | From (2.3) the set of positive roots must have size \(>k\); similarly for negative roots. | Reasoning that if the number of positive roots were \(\le k\) we would obtain a forbidden subset. | Because step 2.3 is invalid, this inference is unsupported. |
| 2.5  | Consequently there exists a subset \(T\) of size \(k+1\) all of the same sign. | Follows from step 2.4. | Since step 2.4 is not justified, the existence of such a \(T\) is not established. |
| 2.6  | Choose any \(k\) elements of \(T\); the resulting monic degree‑\(k\) divisor has all non‑zero coefficients, contradicting (**H**). | This part would be correct **if** such a \(T\) were known to exist. | The contradiction only works if step 2.5 is valid. |

Thus the logical chain collapses at step 2.3 because it misinterprets the hypothesis.

---

**3. Counterexample Hunting**

Consider a polynomial that satisfies the hypothesis but whose all roots are real.  
Take \(n=3,\;k=2\) and  

\[
P(x)=(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+11x-6 .
\]

All roots are real and non‑zero.  
Any real quadratic divisor of \(P\) must be of the form \((x-a)(x-b)\) with \(a,b\in\{1,2,3\}\). The possible quadratics are  

\[
(x-1)(x-2)=x^{2}-3x+2,\qquad
(x-1)(x-3)=x^{2}-4x+3,\qquad
(x-2)(x-3)=x^{2}-5x+6 .
\]

Each of these has **all coefficients non‑zero**, so they violate the hypothesis.  
Thus this polynomial does **not** satisfy the hypothesis, which is consistent with the claim that any \(P\) satisfying the hypothesis must have a non‑real root.  

However, to expose the flaw we need a polynomial that *does* satisfy the hypothesis and has only real roots. Such a polynomial does **not** exist (the theorem we aim to prove), but the proposed proof does not exclude the possibility because it never uses the restriction that the divisor must have degree exactly \(k\). Hence the proof cannot rule out a potential counterexample where every divisor of degree exactly \(k\) has a zero coefficient while a divisor of lower degree does not.

---

**4. Hidden Assumption Check**

The solution implicitly assumes that the hypothesis (**H**) applies to **all** divisors of degree \(\le k\). The problem statement, however, specifies a divisor of *exactly* degree \(k\) (the leading coefficient \(a_k\) is part of the given list of numbers). This hidden strengthening is not justified and is false in general.

Because of this hidden assumption, the deduction that a subset of size \(|S|<k\) consisting of roots of the same sign leads to a contradiction is invalid.

---

**Conclusion of analysis**

The proof’s core idea—using the sign of the roots to obtain a divisor with non‑zero coefficients—is correct, but the execution misapplies the hypothesis to divisors of degree smaller than \(k\). Consequently the argument that at least one sign must appear more than \(k\) times is unsupported, and the claimed contradiction does not follow from the given hypothesis.

Hence the proposed solution is **not correct**.

</ANALYSIS>

**Method sketch:** Assume that all zeros of \(P\) are real and non‑zero.  
If there are at most \(k\) positive (resp. negative) zeros, the monic factor
obtained from those zeros has all coefficients non‑zero, contradicting the
hypothesis. Hence \(P\) must contain at least \(k+1\) zeros of the same sign.
Taking any \(k\) of them gives a degree‑\(k\) divisor whose coefficients are
all non‑zero – again contradicting the hypothesis. Therefore the original
assumption is impossible and \(P\) possesses a non‑real root.

## Detailed Solution  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i), \qquad c\neq 0,
\]

where the \(r_i\)'s are the (distinct) zeros of \(P\); they are real numbers
different from \(0\) because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero.

The hypothesis is  

> (**H**) for every real polynomial  
> \(D(x)=a_kx^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0\) that divides \(P\) (in
> \(\mathbb{R}[x]\)), one has \(a_0a_1\cdots a_k =0\).

We shall prove that (**H**) forces \(P\) to have a non‑real zero.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 1.  Consequence of (**H**) for small‑degree factors

For any subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) let  

\[
Q_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
\]

(the monic polynomial whose zeros are exactly the \(r_i\) with \(i\in S\)).
If \(|S|\le k\), then \(Q_S\) divides \(P\); by (**H**) the product of its
coefficients must be \(0\).

Write  

\[
Q_S(x)=x^{|S|}+e_1(S)x^{|S|-1}+e_2(S)x^{|S|-2}+\dots +e_{|S|}(S),
\tag{1}
\]

where  

\[
e_j(S)=(-1)^j\!\!\sum_{\substack{I\subset S\\|I|=j}}\;\prod_{i\in I} r_i
\qquad (1\le j\le |S|)
\]

are the elementary symmetric sums of the numbers \(\{r_i\mid i\in S\}\)
(up to the sign \((-1)^j\)).  
Thus the constant term of \(Q_S\) is \((-1)^{|S|}\!\!\prod_{i\in S} r_i\).

Consequently, if all the numbers \(r_i\;(i\in S)\) have the **same sign**,
every product \(\prod_{i\in I}r_i\) that appears in an \(e_j(S)\) is positive,
hence each \(e_j(S)\) is **non‑zero**. In particular the product of the
coefficients in (1) is non‑zero.

Therefore, for any subset \(S\) with \(|S|\le k\),

\[
\boxed{\text{If all }r_i\;(i\in S)\text{ have the same sign, then }a_0a_1\cdots a_{|S|}\neq0.}
\tag{2}
\]

Condition (**H**) forces the left‑hand side of (2) to be \(0\); consequently

\[
\tag{3}
\text{No subset }S\text{ with }|S|\le k\text{ may consist of numbers of a single sign.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Existence of many zeros of the same sign

Let  

\[
P_+=\{\,i\mid r_i>0\,\},\qquad P_-=\{\,i\mid r_i<0\,\}.
\]

Denote \(p=|P_+|\) (the number of positive zeros) and \(q=|P_-|=n-p\) (the
number of negative zeros).  

If \(p\le k\), then the set \(S=P_+\) satisfies \(|S|=p\le k\) and all its
elements are positive, contradicting (3).  
Hence **\(p>k\)**. An identical argument shows that either \(p>k\) or
\(q>k\); in any case one of the two signs occurs at least \(k+1\) times.

Consequently there exists a subset \(T\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with  

\[
|T|=k+1,\qquad\text{and either }r_i>0\ \forall i\in T\ \text{or}\ r_i<0\ \forall i\in T.
\tag{4}
\]

Thus we have isolated \(k+1\) distinct zeros of the same sign.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  A degree‑\(k\) divisor contradicting (**H**)

From the \(k+1\) numbers in (4) pick any \(k\) of them; call the chosen
indices \(U\) (\(|U|=k\)).  
The monic polynomial

\[
D(x)=\prod_{i\in U}(x-r_i)
\]

has degree \(k\) and clearly divides \(P\) (its zero set is a subset of the
zero set of \(P\)).  
All zeros of \(D\) have the same sign, hence, by the discussion leading to
(2), **every coefficient of \(D\) is non‑zero**; therefore the product
\(a_0a_1\cdots a_k\neq0\).

But this contradicts hypothesis (**H**), which demands that any degree‑\(k\)
real divisor of \(P\) have at least one zero coefficient.

The contradiction arose from the assumption that all zeros of \(P\) are real
(and non‑zero). Hence this assumption is false.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Conclusion

\(P(x)\) cannot have all its zeros real. Since its constant term is non‑zero,
\(0\) is not a root. Therefore \(P\) possesses at least one **non‑real** root.

\[
\boxed{\text{The polynomial }P\text{ has a non‑real zero.}}
\]

Let \(n>k\ge 1\) be integers.

a_{k}x^{k}+a_{k-1}x^{k-1}+\dots +a_{0}\mid P(x)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_{0}a_{1}\cdots a_{k}=0 .
\tag{H}

1. Write the roots of \(P\) as distinct non‑zero real numbers and translate

2. Prove a combinatorial lemma: *if every \(k\)-element subset of a set of
   distinct non‑zero reals has a vanishing elementary symmetric sum, then at
   least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the same sign*.  
   The lemma is proved by induction on \(k\); the inductive step is made
   rigorous by a careful analysis of the equations that arise from the
   hypothesis.

The earlier proof of the lemma incorrectly asserted the uniqueness of a
certain index.  The new proof treats the two possibilities

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Roots and the reformulated hypothesis  

Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, none of its roots is zero.
Write the distinct roots as  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_i),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_i\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}.
\tag{1}
\]

For a subset \(S\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) put  

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)
      =x^{|S|}+e_1(S)x^{|S|-1}+e_2(S)x^{|S|-2}+\dots+e_{|S|}(S) .
\tag{2}
\]

The numbers \(e_j(S)\;(1\le j\le |S|)\) are the elementary symmetric sums
of the elements \(\{r_i\mid i\in S\}\); by convention
\(e_0(S)=1\).

If \(|S|=k\) then \(D_S\) is a monic divisor of degree exactly \(k\) of \(P\).
Thus hypothesis \((H)\) is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{\text{For every }k\text{-element }S,\;
      \exists\,j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\text{ with }e_j(S)=0.}
\tag{3}
\]

In what follows we assume that all \(r_i\) are real and derive a
contradiction to (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A combinatorial lemma  

> **Lemma 1.**  
> Let \(r_1,\dots ,r_n\) be distinct non‑zero real numbers and let
> \(1\le k<n\).  
> If condition (3) holds for **every** \(k\)-element subset of
> \(\{r_1,\dots ,r_n\}\), then at least \(k+1\) of the numbers have the
> same sign.

We prove the lemma by induction on \(k\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Base \(k=1\)

For a 1‑element set \(\{r_i\}\) we have \(e_1(\{r_i\})=r_i\).  
Condition (3) forces \(r_i=0\), contradicting the hypothesis that the
\(r_i\) are non‑zero.  Hence the premise cannot be satisfied, and the
conclusion “there are at least \(2\) numbers of the same sign’’ is
trivially true.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Inductive step  

Assume the lemma true for \(k-1\) (\(k\ge 2\)).
Suppose (3) holds for the given \(k\) but that **no** sign occurs
\(k+1\) times among the \(r_i\).  Consequently each sign occurs at most
\(k\) times; write  

\[
P=\{i\mid r_i>0\},\qquad N=\{i\mid r_i<0\},
\qquad |P|\le k,\;|N|\le k .
\tag{4}
\]

Let \(A\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}\) be an arbitrary \((k-1)\)-element set and
let \(R=\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus A\); then \(|R|=n-(k-1)\ge 2\) because

For each \(t\in R\) the set \(A\cup\{t\}\) has size \(k\); by (3) there

\[
j(t)\in\{1,\dots ,k\}\quad\text{such that}\quad
e_{j(t)}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=0 .                                          \tag{5}
\]

The elementary symmetric sums satisfy the well‑known recurrence  

\[
e_{j}\bigl(A\cup\{t\}\bigr)=e_{j}(A)+(-1)^{j-1}r_t\,e_{j-1}(A)
\qquad(1\le j\le k).                                          \tag{6}
\]

Insert (6) into (5):

\[
e_{j(t)}(A)+(-1)^{j(t)-1}r_t\,e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0 .
\tag{7}
\]

---

##### Case 1.  For some \(t\in R\) we have \(e_{j(t)-1}(A)=0\).

satisfies condition (3) (with the index \(j(t)-1\) or \(j(t)\)), and we are
done for this particular \(A\).

\[

\tag{8}
\]

Because the numbers \(r_t\) are distinct, the right–hand side must give

\[
j(t)=j_0\qquad\text{for every }t\in R .                                     \tag{9}
\]

\[
e_{j_0}(A)+(-1)^{j_0-1}r_t\,e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                               \tag{10}
\]

\[
e_{j_0-1}(A)=0 .                                                            \tag{11}
\]

If \(j_0=1\) then (11) reads \(e_0(A)=1=0\), impossible; therefore
\(j_0\ge 2\).  Substituting (11) back into (10) yields

\[
e_{j_0}(A)=0 .                                                             \tag{12}
\]

Thus the \((k-1)\)-set \(A\) also satisfies condition (3):
some elementary symmetric sum (namely \(e_{j_0-1}(A)\) or \(e_{j_0}(A)\))
vanishes.

Since the argument applies to **every** \((k-1)\)-element set \(A\),
we have proved:

> **Claim.**  If condition (3) holds for all \(k\)-subsets, then it also
> holds for all \((k-1)\)-subsets.

Applying the induction hypothesis to the family of \((k-1)\)-subsets,
we conclude that at least \(k\) of the numbers \(r_i\) have the same sign.
Because we assumed that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times, exactly
\(k\) numbers share one sign and the remaining \(n-k\) have the opposite
sign.

Now pick a \((k-1)\)-subset \(B\) consisting entirely of those \(k\)
equal‑sign numbers, and let \(t\) be the *remaining* number of the same
sign (it exists because the total number of that sign is \(k\)).  The set
\(B\cup\{t\}\) is a \(k\)-element subset whose elements are **all of the
same sign**.  For a set of numbers with identical sign none of the
elementary symmetric sums can vanish (each term in each sum is a product
of numbers of the same sign and therefore is strictly positive).  This
contradicts (3).

Hence our assumption that no sign occurs \(k+1\) times is untenable, and
the lemma is proved. ∎

### 3.  Construction of a forbidden divisor

Assume, for contradiction, that all roots of \(P\) are real.
Lemma 1 yields a subset  

\[
T=\{i_1,i_2,\dots ,i_{k+1}\}\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

such that the numbers \(r_{i_1},\dots ,r_{i_{k+1}}\) have the same sign.
Choose any \(k\) of them; denote the chosen index set by \(S\) (\(|S|=k\)).
Consider the monic polynomial

\[
D_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_i)

The contradiction arose from the assumption that every root of \(P\) is
real.  Therefore \(P\) must have at least one non‑real zero.  (The constant
term of \(P\) is non‑zero, so \(0\) cannot be a root; the non‑real zero is

ideas.name: Probabilistic alteration of the integer grid
ideas.description: Begin with the √n × √n integer grid, which achieves Θ(n/√log n) distinct distances but contains many squares. Randomly delete each point with a small probability p, then rescale the remaining set to size n. By the Lovász Local Lemma (or simple alteration), with positive probability no square (or other forbidden 4‑point pattern) survives, while the expected number of distinct distances drops only by a factor (1−p)^2, preserving the desired asymptotics.
